title: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
claim: Perception-based state estimates are uncertain, so a single best-guess state can be wrong and make decisions unsafe or infeasible.
layout: 1 panel, egocentric robot view, two callout arrows with probability labels
description: A single full-bleed simulated kitchen image from a robot's viewpoint. A robot arm with a gripper holds a milk carton above a counter that also holds an egg carton, a pitcher and an apple. On the left, an open fridge shows a sandwich and milk cartons on the upper shelves and a kiwi on a lower shelf. Two yellow callout boxes with curved arrows point into the fridge. 'Top Shelf Clear: 60%' points to the upper shelf. 'Bottom Shelf Clear: 95%' points to the lower shelf. The labels show that the perception model is unsure whether a shelf is free for placing the milk. The eye goes first to the robot gripper and milk carton, then to the yellow callouts.

abstract: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $Î¸$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_Î¸$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_Î¸$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_Î¸$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_Î¸$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.
